hook.text: A dog bites a man — not news. A man bites a dog — that's news. But who decides?

buildup.text: News is information that is timely, significant, and relevant to the audience. Not just anything interesting.

discovery.text: Editors use 'news values' — novelty, impact, proximity, conflict, and prominence — to filter stories.

twist.text: What becomes news depends as much on the editor's judgment as on the event itself.

climax.text: News isn't a mirror of reality. It's a curated selection shaped by human choices.

punchline.text: News doesn't show you the world. It shows you a selection.

quiz.question: What are 'news values'?
options: Criteria editors use to decide what becomes news

hook.text: Newspaper stories put the most important facts first. If you only read the headline, you get the gist.

buildup.text: The inverted pyramid structure starts with who, what, when, where, and why — then adds detail.

discovery.text: This format was invented during the Civil War when telegraph lines could cut off mid-message.

twist.text: Online news flipped this — clickbait headlines hide the key fact to force you to click through.

climax.text: The structure of a story tells you whether it's designed to inform or to generate clicks.

punchline.text: Good journalism answers questions. Clickbait withholds them.

quiz.question: Why was the inverted pyramid structure invented?
options: Telegraph lines could cut off mid-message during the Civil War

hook.text: Watergate was broken by two reporters and one anonymous source called 'Deep Throat.'

buildup.text: Journalists rely on sources — officials, witnesses, experts, and documents — to construct stories.

discovery.text: Anonymous sources protect whistleblowers but also allow officials to float ideas without accountability.

twist.text: When you read 'sources say,' ask: who benefits from this information being published right now?

climax.text: Sources aren't neutral. Everyone who talks to a reporter has a reason for talking.

punchline.text: Every source has a motive. Every quote has a purpose.

quiz.question: What should you ask when a news story cites anonymous sources?
options: Who benefits from this information being published?

hook.text: A reporter files a story. An editor rewrites the headline. The story's meaning shifts entirely.

buildup.text: News goes through reporters, editors, copy editors, and layout teams before reaching you.

discovery.text: Headlines are often written by editors, not reporters — and they can distort the article's content.

twist.text: The rise of digital-first newsrooms has compressed this process. Fewer editors means more errors.

climax.text: If a headline and the article disagree, trust the article. The headline was written for clicks.

punchline.text: Read past the headline. The story might disagree with it.

quiz.question: Who typically writes newspaper headlines?
options: The reporter who wrote the story

hook.text: A reporter who covers the Pentagon full-time knows things a general assignment reporter never would.

buildup.text: News beats are specialized areas — politics, health, crime, tech — that reporters cover exclusively.

discovery.text: Beat reporters build deep expertise and source networks that make their coverage more accurate.

twist.text: As newsrooms shrank, beat reporters were cut. Generalists now cover stories they barely understand.

climax.text: The quality of news reporting is directly tied to the expertise of the reporter covering it.

punchline.text: When the expert reporter gets fired, the coverage gets worse.

quiz.question: What happened as newsrooms cut beat reporters?
options: Generalists began covering stories they lacked expertise in

hook.text: Read a local paper's international story? It probably came from the AP or Reuters, not a local reporter.

buildup.text: Wire services are news agencies that supply stories, photos, and video to media outlets worldwide.

discovery.text: AP and Reuters supply content to thousands of outlets. Most 'different' sources share the same original story.

twist.text: When ten outlets run the same story, it looks like confirmation. It's actually the same source ten times.

climax.text: Seeing a story everywhere doesn't mean it's been independently verified. It may be one report, amplified.

punchline.text: Ten outlets, one source. That's not verification. That's echo.

quiz.question: Why can seeing a story in multiple outlets be misleading?
options: They often share the same wire service source

hook.text: A TV news segment averages 90 seconds. In that time, you get the story's emotion, not its complexity.

buildup.text: Television news prioritizes visual stories. If there's no footage, the story often gets skipped.

discovery.text: This visual bias means house fires get covered but policy changes that affect millions don't.

twist.text: 24-hour news channels fill time with opinion shows disguised as news, blurring the line completely.

climax.text: Television news shapes what you think about by deciding what's worth showing you.

punchline.text: TV shows what looks dramatic, not what matters most.

quiz.question: What is the 'visual bias' of television news?
options: It prioritizes stories with footage over important but unvisual stories

hook.text: The New York Times has won 132 Pulitzer Prizes. It still struggles to pay its reporters.

buildup.text: Print journalism was long considered the gold standard — thorough, edited, and accountable.

discovery.text: Newspapers employ fact-checkers and follow editorial standards that digital-first outlets often skip.

twist.text: Print revenue collapsed 80% since 2000 as advertising moved to Google and Facebook.

climax.text: The institutions that produce the most original reporting are the ones struggling hardest to survive.

punchline.text: We need newspapers. We just stopped paying for them.

quiz.question: Why are print newspapers struggling financially?
options: Advertising revenue moved to tech platforms like Google and Facebook

hook.text: BuzzFeed won a Pulitzer for international reporting. Then it shut down its news division.

buildup.text: Online news promised faster, cheaper, and more accessible journalism for everyone.

discovery.text: Digital media relies on clicks for revenue, incentivizing sensational headlines over nuanced reporting.

twist.text: Quality journalism is expensive. Clicks are cheap. The business model punishes depth.

climax.text: Digital news isn't inherently worse. But its economic model pushes it toward clickbait.

punchline.text: Free news isn't free. Someone's paying — and it's probably not you.

quiz.question: How does the click-based revenue model affect online news?
options: It incentivizes sensational headlines over depth
It has no effect on content

hook.text: NPR's 'Up First' delivers the news in 10 minutes each morning. Millions listen while commuting.

buildup.text: Audio news through podcasts and radio reaches people during moments other media can't — driving, walking, cooking.

discovery.text: The intimacy of voice creates trust. Listeners feel they 'know' podcast hosts personally.

twist.text: That sense of trust can be exploited — opinion can feel like fact when delivered by a familiar voice.

climax.text: Audio journalism's strength — personal connection — is also its vulnerability to manipulation.

punchline.text: A trusted voice is powerful. But trust isn't the same as accuracy.

quiz.question: What vulnerability does audio journalism's personal tone create?
options: Opinion can feel like fact from a trusted-sounding voice

hook.text: More Americans under 30 get their news from TikTok than from any news organization.

buildup.text: Social platforms have become primary news sources even though they were designed for socializing, not reporting.

discovery.text: News on social media is filtered by algorithms, friends, and influencers — not by journalistic standards.

twist.text: You think you're choosing your news. The algorithm is choosing it for you based on what keeps you scrolling.

climax.text: When your news source is a feed, the editorial decisions are invisible — and unchallengeable.

punchline.text: The feed isn't random. It's a decision you didn't make.

quiz.question: Why is getting news from social media problematic?
options: Algorithms filter news by engagement, not journalistic standards

hook.text: Substack turned individual journalists into media brands. Some earn over $1 million per year.

buildup.text: Email newsletters bypass algorithms — they deliver directly to your inbox, unfiltered.

discovery.text: This direct relationship means newsletters can go deep on topics mainstream outlets ignore.

twist.text: But newsletters have no editors, fact-checkers, or accountability beyond the writer's reputation.

climax.text: Newsletters are as good as their author — and as biased, unchecked, and imperfect.

punchline.text: No algorithm, no editor. Just one writer and your trust.

quiz.question: What is a key risk of newsletter journalism?
options: They lack editors and institutional fact-checking

hook.text: A professional-looking website claimed a celebrity died. Millions shared it. The celebrity was alive and well.

buildup.text: Checking the source means asking: who published this, and do they have a track record of accuracy?

discovery.text: Reliable sources have bylines, correction policies, editorial standards, and transparent ownership.

twist.text: Unreliable sources often mimic legitimate news design — professional layouts and serious-sounding names.

climax.text: The 'About Us' page tells you more about a news source's reliability than any single article.

punchline.text: Before trusting the story, investigate who's telling it.

quiz.question: What indicates a reliable news source?
options: Bylines, correction policies, and transparent ownership

hook.text: A tweet quotes an article that quotes a study that quotes a researcher. By the fourth layer, the fact is distorted.

buildup.text: Primary sources are original documents, data, or eyewitness accounts. Secondary sources interpret or report on them.

discovery.text: Each layer of reporting adds interpretation and potential distortion to the original information.

twist.text: Most viral news is secondary or tertiary — several layers removed from the original facts.

climax.text: Tracing a claim back to its primary source is the single most powerful fact-checking skill.

punchline.text: Follow the chain back. The original source tells a different story.

quiz.question: Why is tracing claims to primary sources important?
options: Each layer of reporting can add distortion

hook.text: Snopes started as one couple fact-checking urban legends from their apartment. Now it's a global resource.

buildup.text: Fact-checking organizations like Snopes, PolitiFact, and FactCheck.org verify claims made in public discourse.

discovery.text: They rate claims on scales from 'True' to 'Pants on Fire' using documented evidence and transparent methods.

twist.text: Fact-checkers are accused of bias by the people they fact-check — which is exactly what you'd expect.

climax.text: No fact-checker is perfect. But their transparent methodology makes them more accountable than social media.

punchline.text: The ones calling fact-checkers biased rarely show their own sources.

quiz.question: What makes fact-checking organizations more reliable than social media?

hook.text: Fact-checkers spend less time on a website than students — because they immediately open new tabs to verify.

buildup.text: Lateral reading means leaving a source's website to check what others say about it, instead of evaluating it in isolation.

discovery.text: Stanford researchers found that professional fact-checkers use lateral reading while students read vertically.

twist.text: A polished website can fool vertical readers. Lateral readers quickly find if the source is legitimate.

climax.text: The fastest way to evaluate a source isn't reading more of it — it's checking what others say about it.

punchline.text: Don't read deeper. Read wider.

quiz.question: What is lateral reading?
options: Reading more content on the same website
Leaving the site to check what others say about the source
Reading news in a foreign language

hook.text: Tucker Carlson's lawyers argued in court that no reasonable viewer would take his show as factual news.

buildup.text: News reports facts. Opinion interprets them. The problem is when opinion is presented as straight news.

discovery.text: News uses neutral language and attributes claims. Opinion uses first person and emotional framing.

twist.text: Many viewers can't tell the difference — 24-hour channels mix news and opinion in the same broadcast.

climax.text: If a news program makes you angry, it's probably opinion. News informs; opinion provokes.

punchline.text: News tells you what happened. Opinion tells you how to feel about it.

quiz.question: How can you distinguish news from opinion?
options: News is always on the front page
News uses neutral language while opinion uses emotional framing

hook.text: A 'Harvard doctor' quoted in a health article turns out to be a dentist commenting outside his field.

buildup.text: News stories quote experts to add credibility. But not all experts are equally qualified on every topic.

discovery.text: Check an expert's specific field, published research, institutional affiliation, and potential conflicts of interest.

twist.text: Media often uses the same few experts repeatedly because they give good quotes, not because they're the most qualified.

climax.text: A real expert speaks cautiously within their field. A media expert speaks confidently about everything.

punchline.text: An expert in one field is a layperson in another. Check the match.

quiz.question: How should you evaluate an expert quoted in news?
options: Check their specific field, research, affiliation, and potential conflicts
Experts are always right in any field

hook.text: For a century, newspapers were cheap because advertisers paid the bills. Then the internet stole those ads.

buildup.text: The advertising model meant news was subsidized — readers paid a fraction of the cost of producing it.

discovery.text: When ad revenue moved to Google and Facebook, newsrooms lost 60% of their staff in two decades.

twist.text: Ad-supported news must attract eyeballs. That incentivizes sensationalism over substance.

climax.text: The business model of news directly shapes the quality of information in a democracy.

punchline.text: Who pays for the news decides what the news is.

quiz.question: How did the shift of advertising to tech platforms affect newsrooms?
options: They lost approximately 60% of their staff

hook.text: The New York Times has 10 million digital subscribers. Most local papers have almost none.

buildup.text: Paywalls ask readers to pay directly, aligning incentives — the news serves you, not advertisers.

discovery.text: Subscription models reward quality because subscribers cancel if the content isn't worth paying for.

twist.text: But paywalls also create an information divide — quality news becomes available only to those who can afford it.

climax.text: In a democracy, limiting access to reliable information based on income is a serious problem.

punchline.text: Good news costs money. Not everyone has it.

quiz.question: What problem do news paywalls create?
options: Quality information becomes accessible only to those who can pay

hook.text: The BBC is funded by a license fee paid by every UK household with a TV. No advertisers needed.

buildup.text: Public broadcasters like BBC, PBS, and NHK are funded by taxes or fees, not advertising revenue.

discovery.text: Without advertiser pressure, public media can cover stories that aren't commercially attractive.

twist.text: Critics argue public funding makes these outlets beholden to government. Independence is never guaranteed.

climax.text: Every funding model creates dependencies. The question is which dependency produces the least bias.

punchline.text: No funding model is neutral. The question is which bias you prefer.

quiz.question: What is the main advantage of publicly funded news?
options: It can cover stories without advertiser pressure

hook.text: ProPublica operates as a nonprofit. It has won six Pulitzer Prizes doing investigative journalism.

buildup.text: Nonprofit news organizations are funded by donations and grants, removing the profit motive.

discovery.text: This model allows long, expensive investigations that ad-supported media can't justify economically.

twist.text: But donors have interests too. Nonprofits must maintain editorial independence from their funders.

climax.text: The best nonprofit newsrooms publish donor lists and editorial independence policies to build trust.

punchline.text: No advertisers, no subscribers. Just donors and a mission.

quiz.question: What advantage do nonprofit news organizations have?
options: They can pursue expensive investigations without profit pressure

hook.text: You read an article about the best travel destinations. It was paid for by an airline. You couldn't tell.

buildup.text: Native advertising is paid content designed to look and feel like genuine editorial content.

discovery.text: Labels like 'sponsored content' or 'paid partnership' are required — but they're often tiny and easily missed.

twist.text: Studies show readers often can't distinguish native ads from real journalism, even when labeled.

climax.text: When advertising disguises itself as news, it erodes the trust that real journalism depends on.

punchline.text: If it looks like news but someone paid for it, it's an ad.

quiz.question: What is native advertising?
options: Paid content designed to look like genuine editorial content

hook.text: Since 2005, the U.S. has lost over 2,500 newspapers. Entire communities have no local news coverage.

buildup.text: News deserts are areas with no local newspaper, TV station, or dedicated news outlet.

discovery.text: Research shows that when local news disappears, government corruption increases and civic engagement drops.

twist.text: National news can't replace local coverage. Nobody in New York reports on your city council meeting.

climax.text: Local journalism is the foundation of democratic accountability — and it's collapsing.

punchline.text: Without local news, nobody watches the people in power.

quiz.question: What happens when local news disappears?
options: Government corruption increases and civic engagement drops

hook.text: If you only eat candy, your body suffers. If you only read one news source, your mind does too.

buildup.text: A balanced news diet includes multiple sources with different perspectives, formats, and ownership.

discovery.text: Mix national with local, print with audio, mainstream with independent. Diversity of source builds accuracy.

twist.text: Most people read fewer than three news sources. Their worldview is shaped by a narrow slice of reality.

climax.text: You don't need to read everything. You need to read enough different things to spot the gaps.

punchline.text: One source gives you a story. Multiple sources give you the truth.

quiz.question: What is a balanced news diet?
options: Reading only one trusted source thoroughly
Consuming multiple sources with different perspectives and formats

hook.text: MIT found that false news stories spread six times faster than true ones on social media.

buildup.text: The impulse to share outrageous news instantly is powerful — but speed is the enemy of accuracy.

discovery.text: Simply pausing to read beyond the headline before sharing reduces misinformation spread dramatically.

twist.text: Platforms know this but don't add friction because friction reduces engagement — and engagement means revenue.

climax.text: The most powerful thing you can do for media quality is pause before you share.

punchline.text: Read it first. Share it second. Or don't share it at all.

quiz.question: According to MIT research, how much faster does false news spread than true news?

hook.text: Democracy requires informed citizens. Informed citizens require funded journalism. The math is simple.

buildup.text: Subscribing, donating, and sharing quality journalism all contribute to its survival.

discovery.text: The cost of one digital news subscription is less than a single coffee per week.

twist.text: We pay for entertainment without thinking. We resist paying for the information that keeps society functioning.

climax.text: If we don't fund journalism directly, we get the news that advertisers and algorithms choose for us.

punchline.text: If you won't pay for news, someone else will decide what you hear.

quiz.question: Why is directly funding journalism important?
options: Without reader support, news is shaped by advertisers and algorithms

hook.text: A teenager gets 90% of her news from TikTok. None of the creators are journalists. She can't tell.

buildup.text: Young people increasingly get news from social media creators rather than established news organizations.

discovery.text: News literacy for young people means learning to evaluate credibility regardless of the platform or format.

twist.text: Schools teach math and reading but rarely teach students how to evaluate the information they consume daily.

climax.text: The generation raised on social media needs media literacy most and receives it least.

punchline.text: If you learn news from TikTok, learn how to verify it too.

quiz.question: Why is news literacy especially important for young people?
options: They increasingly consume news from social media creators without verification skills

hook.text: When the local paper closed, the town council quietly doubled its own salaries. Nobody was watching.

buildup.text: Local news covers schools, courts, and government that directly affect your daily life.

discovery.text: Research shows local news deserts lead to higher government borrowing costs, less civic engagement, and more corruption.

twist.text: Over 2,500 local newspapers have closed since 2005. Millions of people live in news deserts with no local coverage.

climax.text: National news can't replace local coverage. The issues closest to you need journalists closest to you.

punchline.text: When local news dies, local power goes unchecked. Support your local paper.

quiz.question: What happens when local newspapers close?
options: Government corruption increases and civic engagement decreases

hook.text: AI can now write news articles in seconds. It can also fabricate them with equal ease.

buildup.text: Newsrooms are experimenting with AI for summaries and data analysis, freeing reporters for deeper work.

discovery.text: But AI-generated news lacks accountability — when AI makes a mistake, who's responsible?

twist.text: The future likely combines human judgment with AI efficiency — but trust will depend on transparency.

climax.text: News literacy will only become more critical as the line between human and machine content blurs.

punchline.text: AI writes faster. Humans verify better. We need both.

quiz.question: What is the main challenge with AI-generated news?
options: It lacks accountability when errors occur
